summary: Describes LDIF, a text file format for describing directory entries or changes to them. It is widely used to import, export and modify LDAP directory data. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A plain text list that says what to put in a directory, like an address book written down line by line, so it can be loaded or backed up.

questions: how to fold lines in ldif
subtitle: A plain text file format for describing LDAP directory entries, or a list of changes to apply to them.

tldr.problem: There was no common file format for moving directory data between LDAP-based servers, or for describing changes to a directory.
tldr.mechanism: LDIF is a line-based text format. A file is a series of records, each starting with a distinguished name, followed by either attribute values or a change record (add, delete, modify, modrdn).
tldr.outcome: LDIF can be produced by simple scripts and imported into any directory server. Because it can pull in external files and carries no authentication, files from outside sources need care.

today: RFC 2849 is a Proposed Standard from June 2000, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Background
sections.content:
LDIF, the LDAP Data Interchange Format, is a file format for describing directory information or modifications made to directory information. It is typically used to import and export directory information between LDAP-based directory servers, or to describe a set of changes to be applied to a directory.

The RFC gives two motivating cases. One is exporting the contents of a directory server to a file, moving it to another machine and importing it into a second server. The other is converting legacy data: a fairly simple set of tools written in awk or perl can turn a personnel database into an LDIF file for any directory server, whatever its internal representation.

LDIF was originally developed and used in the University of Michigan LDAP implementation. It first described directory entries and was later expanded to describe changes. It is a simpler alternative to the application/directory MIME content-type, which is a general framework independent of any directory service.
sections.eli5: It is a plain list that any program can write, so you can copy a directory from one computer to another.

sections.title: Records and Files
sections.content:
An LDIF file is a series of records separated by line separators. A record is a sequence of lines describing either a directory entry or a set of changes to one entry. A file specifies entries or changes, but not both.

Every record starts with a dn: line giving the distinguished name, and the file starts with version: 1. The version number MUST be 1. If it is absent, an implementation MAY treat the file as the older University of Michigan ldap-3.3 format.

Each attribute value line has the form name: value, and an attribute may carry options, such as ou;lang-ja for a language tag.
sections.eli5: The file is a stack of cards. Each card starts with the name of an entry and then lists facts about it.

sections.title: Syntax Rules
sections.content:
The grammar is given in ABNF. The notes attached to it set the rules that matter in practice:

  • Folding: any non-empty line MAY be folded by inserting a line separator and a single space. A line starting with one space continues the previous line, and exactly one leading space is dropped when joining.
  • Comments: lines beginning with the pound sign MUST be ignored.
  • Base64: a value, DN or RDN containing characters outside the SAFE-CHAR set, or starting with a character outside SAFE-INIT-CHAR, MUST be base64 encoded. This is marked by a double colon, as in description:: .... Values ending with a space SHOULD be base64 encoded.
  • UTF-8: DNs, RDNs and DirectoryString values MUST be valid UTF-8, and implementations MUST NOT generate anything else.
  • Empty values: a zero-length value is written as the attribute name, a colon and nothing more.
  • URLs: name:< url includes the content the URL names. Implementations SHOULD support file:// URLs and MAY support others.

Base64 here follows RFC 2045 with two exceptions: there is no 76 character line limit (LDIF folding rules apply instead), and no extraneous characters are allowed except for folding.
sections.eli5: If a line has a tricky letter in it, you scramble it into plain letters and numbers first. Long lines can be broken, with a space starting the next piece.

sections.title: Change Records
sections.content:
A change record has a changetype: line. There is a one-to-one match with the LDAP operations that modify a directory, which allows a straightforward translation to protocol operations. The types are:

  • add: lists the attributes of the new entry.
  • delete: removes the entry.
  • modrdn or moddn: gives a newrdn, a deleteoldrdn of 0 or 1, and optionally a newsuperior to move the entry.
  • modify: a series of add:, delete: or replace: blocks, each ended by a line holding a single hyphen.

A record may also start with control: lines carrying an OID, an optional criticality of true or false and an optional value. Implementations MAY ignore controls, for example on an LDAPv2 connection. If a control is critical (true), the implementation MUST either include it or MUST NOT send the operation to the remote server.
sections.eli5: Instead of a whole address book, this file can be a to-do list: add this person, remove that one, change this phone number.

sections.title: Examples in the RFC
sections.content:
The RFC gives seven examples: a simple file with two entries, a folded value, a base64-encoded value, UTF-8 values with language tags (with comments showing what the encoded text means), a reference to an external file, a series of change records, and a change record with a control.

The last example deletes an entry using the Tree Delete Control, with criticality set to true. The RFC cites that control as work in progress.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows seven sample files so you can see what the rules look like in real life.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An LDIF file is likely to contain sensitive personal data, so appropriate measures should be taken to protect the privacy of the people it describes.

The :< directive can include external content, so be cautious of accepting LDIF files from external sources. A trojan LDIF file could name a file with sensitive contents and have it included in a directory entry that a hostile entity could read via LDAP.

LDIF has no way to carry authentication information with the file, so users must verify the integrity of a file received from an external source.
sections.eli5: A list of people's details is private, and a list that says "copy this other file in" could trick you into sharing something secret. Only trust lists from people you know.

viz.caption: LDIF CHANGE RECORDS (FROM EXAMPLE 6 IN THE RFC)

data.title: Add, delete and rename
data.code:
version: 1
# Add a new entry
dn: cn=Fiona Jensen, ou=Marketing, dc=airius, dc=com
changetype: add
objectclass: top
objectclass: person
objectclass: organizationalPerson
cn: Fiona Jensen
sn: Jensen

# Delete an existing entry
dn: cn=Robert Jensen, ou=Marketing, dc=airius, dc=com
changetype: delete

# Modify an entry's relative distinguished name
dn: cn=Paul Jensen, ou=Product Development, dc=airius, dc=com
changetype: modrdn
newrdn: cn=Paula Jensen
deleteoldrdn: 1

items.label: Add entry
items.desc: Lists the attribute values of a new entry.

items.label: Delete entry
items.desc: Removes the entry named by the dn.

items.label: Modify entry
items.desc: Blocks of add:, delete: or replace:, each ended by a lone hyphen.

items.label: Rename or move
items.desc: Uses newrdn, deleteoldrdn and optionally newsuperior.
